{{Short description|Theorem about the radii of convergence of power series}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Cauchy–Hadamard theorem''' is a result in [[complex analysis]] named after the [[France|French]] [[mathematician]]s [[Augustin Louis Cauchy]] and [[Jacques Hadamard]], describing the [[radius of convergence]] of a [[power series]]. It was published in 1821 by Cauchy,<ref>{{citation|first=A. L.|last=Cauchy|author-link=Augustin Louis Cauchy|title=Analyse algébrique|year=1821}}.</ref> but remained relatively unknown until Hadamard rediscovered it.<ref>{{citation|title=The Higher Calculus: A History of Real and Complex Analysis from Euler to Weierstrass|first=Umberto|last=Bottazzini|author-link=Umberto Bottazzini| publisher=Springer-Verlag|year=1986|isbn=978-0-387-96302-0|pages=[https://archive.org/details/highercalculushi0000bott/page/116 116–117]|url=https://archive.org/details/highercalculushi0000bott/page/116}}. Translated from the Italian by Warren Van Egmond.</ref> Hadamard's first publication of this result was in 1888;<ref>{{citation|first=J.|last=Hadamard|author-link=Jacques Hadamard|title=Sur le rayon de convergence des séries ordonnées suivant les puissances d'une variable|journal=C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris|volume=106|pages=259–262}}.</ref> he also included it as part of his 1892 Ph.D. thesis.<ref>{{citation| first=J.|last=Hadamard|author-link=Jacques Hadamard|title=Essai sur l'étude des fonctions données par leur développement de Taylor| url=https://archive.org/details/essaisurltuded00hadauoft| journal=[[Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées]]|series= 4<sup>e</sup> Série|volume=VIII|year=1892}}. Also in ''Thèses présentées à la faculté des sciences de Paris pour obtenir le grade de docteur ès sciences mathématiques'', Paris: Gauthier-Villars et fils, 1892.</ref>

==Theorem for one complex variable==
Consider the formal [[power series]] in one complex variable ''z'' of the form
<math display="block">f(z) = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} c_{n} (z-a)^{n}</math>
where <math>a, c_n \in \Complex.</math>

Then the [[radius of convergence]] <math>R</math> of ''f'' at the point ''a'' is given by
<math display="block">\frac{1}{R} = \limsup_{n \to \infty} \left( | c_{n} |^{1/n} \right)</math>
where {{math|lim sup}} denotes the [[limit superior]], the limit as {{mvar|n}} approaches infinity of the [[supremum]] of the sequence values after the ''n''th position. If the sequence values is unbounded so that the {{math|lim sup}} is ∞, then the power series does not converge near {{math|''a''}}, while if the {{math|lim sup}} is 0 then the radius of convergence is ∞, meaning that the series converges on the entire plane.

===Proof===
[[Without loss of generality]] assume that <math>a=0</math>. We will show first that the power series <math display="inline">\sum_n c_n z^n</math> converges for <math>|z|<R</math>, and then that it diverges for <math>|z|>R</math>.

First suppose <math>|z|<R</math>. Let <math>t=1/R</math> not be <math>0</math> or <math>\pm\infty.</math>
For any <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>, there exists only a finite number of <math>n</math> such that <math display="inline">\sqrt[n]{|c_n|} \geq t+\varepsilon</math>. 
Now <math>|c_n| < (t+\varepsilon)^n</math> for all but a finite number of <math>c_n</math>, so the series <math display="inline">\sum_n c_n z^n</math> converges if <math>|z| < 1/(t+\varepsilon)</math>. This proves the first part.

Conversely, for <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>, <math>|c_n|\geq (t-\varepsilon)^n</math> for infinitely many <math>c_n</math>, so if <math>|z|=1/(t-\varepsilon) > R</math>, we see that the series cannot converge because its ''n''th term does not tend to 0.<ref>{{citation|title=Complex Analysis: Fourth Edition|first=Serge|last=Lang| publisher=Springer|year=2002| isbn=0-387-98592-1|pages=55–56}} Graduate Texts in Mathematics</ref>

==Theorem for several complex variables==
Let <math>\alpha</math> be an ''n''-dimensional vector of natural numbers (<math>\alpha = (\alpha_1, \cdots, \alpha_n) \in \N^n</math>) with <math>\|\alpha\| := \alpha_1 + \cdots + \alpha_n</math>, then <math>f(z)</math> converges with radius of convergence <math>\rho = (\rho_1, \cdots, \rho_n) \in \R^n</math>, <math>\rho^\alpha = \rho_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots \rho_n^{\alpha_n}</math> [[if and only if]]
<math display="block">\limsup_{\|\alpha\|\to\infty} \sqrt[\|\alpha\|]{|c_\alpha|\rho^\alpha}=1</math>
of the multidimensional power series
<math display="block"> f(z) = \sum_{\alpha\geq0}c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha := \sum_{\alpha_1\geq0,\ldots,\alpha_n\geq0}c_{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n}(z_1-a_1)^{\alpha_1}\cdots(z_n-a_n)^{\alpha_n}.</math>

===Proof===
From <ref>{{citation| title=Introduction to complex analysis Part II. Functions of several variables| first=B. V.| last=Shabat| publisher=American Mathematical Society| year=1992| isbn=978-0821819753| pages=32–33}}</ref>

Set <math>z = a + t\rho</math> <math>(z_i = a_i + t\rho_i).</math> Then

:<math>\sum_{\alpha \geq 0} c_\alpha (z - a)^\alpha = \sum_{\alpha \geq 0} c_\alpha \rho^\alpha t^{\|\alpha\|} = \sum_{\mu \geq 0} \left( \sum_{\|\alpha\| = \mu} |c_\alpha| \rho^\alpha \right) t^\mu. </math>

This is a power series in one variable <math>t</math> which converges for <math>|t| < 1</math> and diverges for <math>|t| > 1</math>. Therefore, by the Cauchy–Hadamard theorem for one variable

:<math>\limsup_{\mu \to \infty} \sqrt[\mu]{\sum_{\|\alpha\| = \mu} |c_\alpha| \rho^\alpha} = 1.</math>

Setting <math>|c_m| \rho^m = \max_{\|\alpha\| = \mu} |c_\alpha| \rho^\alpha</math> gives us an estimate

:<math>|c_m| \rho^m \leq \sum_{\|\alpha\| = \mu} |c_\alpha| \rho^\alpha \leq (\mu + 1)^n |c_m| \rho^m. </math>

Because <math>\sqrt[\mu]{(\mu + 1)^n} \to 1</math> as <math>\mu \to \infty</math>

:<math>\sqrt[\mu]{|c_m| \rho^m} \leq \sqrt[\mu]{\sum_{\|\alpha\| = \mu} |c_\alpha| \rho^\alpha} \leq \sqrt[\mu]{|c_m| \rho^m} \implies \sqrt[\mu]{\sum_{\|\alpha\| = \mu} |c_\alpha| \rho^\alpha} = \sqrt[\mu]{|c_m| \rho^m} \qquad (\mu \to \infty). </math>

Therefore

:<math>\limsup_{\|\alpha\|\to\infty} \sqrt[\|\alpha\|]{|c_\alpha|\rho^\alpha} = \limsup_{\mu \to \infty} \sqrt[\mu]{|c_m| \rho^m} = 1.</math>
